# Writing instruction files coding agents follow

How to author the files an AI coding agent reads — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, an
agent or automation spec — so it follows them reliably. Grounded entirely in Anthropic's
published guidance; bracketed numbers cite the sources listed at the end.

## Know what an instruction file is (and isn't)

- Treat the file as context, not enforced configuration: the agent reads it and tries to
  follow it, with no guarantee of strict compliance. Anything that must happen every time
  (block a write, run a linter before commit) belongs in a deterministic hook instead. [1][2]
- Everything loaded at session start competes for a finite attention budget, and recall
  degrades as context grows ("context rot"). Aim for the smallest set of high-signal tokens
  that produces the behavior you want. [4]
- Keep the always-loaded file to facts that apply broadly in every session. Move multi-step
  procedures and sometimes-relevant domain knowledge into on-demand skills, and rules that
  matter for only part of the codebase into path-scoped rule files. [1][2]

## Decide each line's right to exist

- Include what the agent can't infer from code: build and test commands, style rules that
  differ from language defaults, repo etiquette (branch naming, PR conventions),
  project-specific architecture decisions, required env vars, non-obvious gotchas. [2]
- Exclude what it can figure out by reading code: standard conventions, file-by-file codebase
  descriptions, detailed API docs (link instead), frequently changing facts, and self-evident
  practices like "write clean code". [2]
- For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause the agent to make mistakes?" If not, cut it.
  Bloated instruction files cause the agent to ignore the instructions that matter. [2]
- Target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md; longer files consume more context and reduce
  adherence. Splitting into imports organizes but does not save context — imports still load
  at launch. [1]

## Write each rule

- Be concrete enough to verify: "Use 2-space indentation", not "Format code properly";
  "Run `npm test` before committing", not "Test your changes". [1]
- Apply the golden rule: show the instruction to a colleague with minimal context — if they'd
  be confused, the agent will be too. [3]
- State the motivation behind a rule, not just the rule; the model generalizes from the
  explanation. [3]
- Tell the agent what to do instead of what not to do: "write flowing prose paragraphs"
  steers better than "do not use markdown". [3]
- Use numbered steps when the order or completeness of steps matters. [3]
- Prefer a few (3–5) diverse, canonical examples over a laundry list of edge-case rules, and
  wrap them in `<example>` tags so they can't be mistaken for instructions. [3][4]
- Pitch rules at the right altitude: specific enough to guide behavior, flexible enough to
  leave the model strong heuristics — avoiding both brittle hardcoded if-then logic and vague
  guidance that assumes shared context. [4]
- Reserve emphasis ("IMPORTANT", "YOU MUST") for tuning adherence on rules that slip. [2]

## Shape a rule so it fires

House practice rather than published guidance — the rest of this file cites its sources, and
this section has none. It is how the rules in this corpus's `RULES.md` files are phrased.

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it.
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets.
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change.
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it.
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
  hand-built command. Measured on two adjacent instructions in one spec: the one naming a file
  was got right first try 0 runs in 5, the one shipping a fenced command 5 in 5.
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause.
- **Carrying the evidence a rule came from** — dates, issue and session ids, quoted exchanges and
  the story of the incident are archaeology, and the commit that added the rule keeps them. Keep a
  measurement only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the reader wouldn't believe stated
  qualitatively ("the retry ran to 81% of a session's tool wall-clock"). A rule that reads as a
  post-mortem with a directive at the top is the wrong way round.
- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
  teaches a world the reader won't find.
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.

## Structure the file

- Group related rules under markdown headers and bullets; the agent scans structure the way
  readers do, and organized sections are easier to follow than dense paragraphs. [1]
- Separate content types — background, instructions, tool guidance, output format — into
  distinct sections with consistent, descriptive names (Markdown headers or XML tags). [3][4]
- Make a task spec self-contained: name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out

# Tasks — a repo's unit of Claudinite work

A **task** is a unit of work a repo does to itself, declared in code and executed in the
repo's own GitHub Actions run. Most tasks are a deterministic script; some also need an
agent. Some recur on a clock; others exist only to be created by hand or by another task.
None of that is in the definition — a task is the declaration plus the work, and everything
else is how one particular occurrence got started.

An occurrence of a task is a **work item**: a GitHub issue titled `[claudinite-work]
<pack>/<task>`, whose number is its identity. The queue *is* the repo's issue list — no
plan file, no watermark, no ledger. The engine is vendored under
`.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`; the basics pack owns the conformance guards for the
surfaces a repo authors around it, present wherever basics is declared (everywhere).

## Four roles, strictly separated

1. **The generator** — a thin scheduled tick. Deterministic label mechanics over the issue
   list: *instantiate* each recurring task's standing item when its anchor comes, *ready*
   blocked items whose dependencies resolved and whose `Not-before` has passed, and
   *reclaim* dead executor claims. It evaluates no preconditions, collects no signals, and
   executes nothing.
2. **Executors** — pull workers, any number of them. Each iteration picks the next ready
   item (urgent first), claims it, evaluates the precondition — the only place it is ever
   evaluated — then runs the work step and either finishes the item or hands it to an
   agent. A no-go rolls the item to its next anchor. An executor's whole interface is issue
   read/write plus the repo at HEAD; more capacity is more executors.
3. **Agents** — one session per handed-off item, invoked by the executor. An agent executes
   its one item's task file, verifies its outcome ceiling, and converges the item.
4. **The janitor** — dead executor claims, dead agent claims, stale-item escalation, queue
   health review.

The tick and a drain run as two jobs of one workflow, in order: the drain picks up what the
tick just created, which is what holds common-case latency at zero without depending on a
label event being delivered.

## The work step is code; the agent is the escalation

An executor that reaches a task's work step runs its `prework` command as a subprocess,
Action-side. When that command finishes without requesting an agent, the executor **closes
the item there** — the run is complete, no session was started, and the item records
whether it left a live artifact. A task with `agent_model: 'none'` is exactly this and
nothing else, which makes it the ordinary way to run a deterministic job in Actions without
authoring a workflow for it.

An agentic task (`agent_model !== 'none'`) declares `agent_instructions`, the worker file
its agent reads. A task may also do both: prework does what it can and escalates the
remainder by requesting the agentic phase (`CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`) — for **work prework
could not do**, never for a re-check of whether the run should have happened.

Because prework runs Action-side, repo Actions secrets are reachable there and nowhere else
in a task's life (an agent session carries none). A task lists what it needs in
`required_secrets`; the wiring converge stamps each name into the workflow, so a worker
reads it as ordinary environment, and baselining asks the owner for any the repo hasn't
configured. Nothing fails when one is missing — the task just doesn't work yet. The
consequence worth designing around: **a workflow that exists only to hold a secret is
redundant** — fold its work into prework rather than dispatching and polling a second
workflow.

## Where an item comes from

Creating an item, or waking one that exists, is the whole mechanism. Four origins, equal in
standing:

- **A recurring task's anchor** — the tick instantiates the standing item. `frequency`
  (`hourly | daily-2h | daily-1h | daily | daily+1h | weekly | monthly`) picks the anchor
  against the repo's `taskScheduler` schedule.
- **By hand** — `create-work-item <pack>/<task> [--urgent] [--context …] [--supersedes #N]`
  writes an item with the generic "forced by hand — no precondition asserts there is work"
  context. It warns when an open same-title item exists, because the pick-time mutex means
  the new one queues behind it rather than jumping.
- **A `wake` dispatch** — the scheduler workflow's one input takes task ids and wakes each
  one's standing item regardless of its anchor, minting the item when none is open. This is
  how a force reaches **across** repos: the fleet enforcer dispatches the member's own
  scheduler and the member applies the recipe with its own token, rather than the enforcer
  holding issue writes on every repository.
- **Another task** — a fan-out creates one item per target, qualified by name
  (`[claudinite-work] sheepdog/fleet-baseline member-repo-x`).

`frequency: 'manual'` is a task the tick never instantiates: its items come only from the
other three. Declaring it is how you say "this task has work when someone says so", and it
costs nothing when nobody does.

Whatever the origin, the executor evaluates the precondition at pick. A force that finds no
work rolls the item with its reason on record, where an operator reads it. A task that must
run unconditionally says so in a Context line its own precondition honors.

## The task folder

One directory per task — `<pack>/tasks/<name>/` — holding **`task.mjs`** (the self-contained
declaration plus `precondition(signals, config)`) beside the worker: a sibling `.mjs` the
prework command runs, a **`task.md`** the agent follows, or both. The precondition both
asserts need-to-run and pre-decides scope: its `context` lines land verbatim in the item as
binding constraints the agent may not re-litigate.

`task.mjs` default-exports `id` (matching its directory), `frequency`,
`precondition_signals` (the collector vocabulary), `agent_model` (`opus | sonnet | haiku |
none`), `expected_outcome` (`none | open-pr | merged-pr` — a declared write **ceiling**, not
a promise), and a `precondition`. The executor reads every one of these from this file and
never from the item, so an illegal or missing value means a task never fires, fires wrong,
or writes past its ceiling. `engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs` is the single definition,
validated by both the author-time check and the executor, so the two views cannot drift.

A task declares **no session scope**. An executor's reach is how its repo was provisioned —
the fleet enforcer's spans the fleet because that repo *is* the enforcer, not because a task
asked for it. The `session_scope` field is deprecated and still honoured: a lingering
`'fleet'` routes to `ready-for-agent-fleet`, whose broader executor routine exists only in
the canon repo, and the canon's curation tasks are the one standing use. Everything else
drops the field.

### Optional declarations

Declare one only when its rule applies.

- **`prework` + `prework_timeout`** — the work-step command (a script beside `task.mjs`, no
  absolute path and no `..`) and the seconds after which it is killed. The timeout must stay
  under the executor's one-hour claim leash: a prework allowed to outlive it is reclaimed
  while still running and the item livelocks. Split the work rather than raise the timeout.
- **`agent_execution_timeout`** — seconds bounding an agentic run. There is no platform
  wall-clock kill for a launched session, so this is best-effort: it reaches the agent as
  "fail after N minutes" and the stale-claim backstop catches a dead one. Set it generously;
  it is protection against a runaway, not a scheduling knob.
- **`after: ['<pack>/<task>']`** — yield while a named upstream's item is live this cycle,
  and pick up the moment it converges or rolls. Declare it when your task reads what another
  produces; never as a general priority hint. It is not a `Blocked-by` edge.
- **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`** (default `requeue`) — declare `needs-human`
  only for a genuinely one-shot side effect (a store submission, an external notification):
  it makes every recovery path that would re-execute the task converge to triage instead.
- **`invocation_endpoint: '<name>'`** — a key into the repo's `taskScheduler.endpoints`, for
  a task whose agentic phase needs reach the repo's ordinary sessions lack. **Never a URL**:
  a task declaration is vendored verbatim into every consuming repo, so deployment detail and
  anything adjacent to a credential stay in that repo's own config.

## The precondition is the ONLY decision point

A task that passes its precondition **runs**. Neither the work step nor the agentic phase
may find new reasons to skip — not timing, not repo state, not "already handled", not an
open PR elsewhere. If a condition should stop the run, it belongs in the precondition, as
code over signals, its verdict binding via the item's Context.

- **Failures may stop a run** — a crash, a timeout, an API error converge to `needs-human`.
  Discretion may not.
- **"The work ran and produced nothing" is always legal** — that is an empty outcome, not a
  skip. The line: did the phase *do* the work and find it empty, or *decline* to do it?

Gate on the objects' own movement in the window, never on standing state, which is true
forever once true. The `task-phase-discipline` world check (advisory, heuristic) hunts for
tasks that escape this — skip-language in `task.md`, cycle-skip strings in prework workers.

### A precondition may claim the whole run

A verdict can carry **`exclusive: true`** beside `run: true` — *if I run this cycle, I run
alone*. Every other due task whose precondition said run is deferred. It exists because a
scheduled tick is not punctual (see the `github-actions-scheduling` skill): a tick that
fires hours late finds several daily anchors at once, so the staging between them collapses
and a task anchored to run *before* the others runs *beside* them.

Claim sparingly, and **bound the claim at both ends**. A deferred item is spent, not queued:
that task runs again at its *next* anchor — tomorrow, or next week. A claim on the routine
case quietly halves throughput, and a claim with no upper bound stops the repo doing
anything for as long as the breakage lasts. Baselining is the model: claim when the mount is
more than a day stale, stop claiming past three days, when it is a human's problem rather
than a missed fire.

## Labels are a scheduler vocabulary

State lives in labels: `task:blocked`, `task:ready`, `task:urgent`, `task:executing`,
`task:agent`, terminal `outcome:done` / `outcome:delivered` / `outcome:obsolete`, and
`needs-human`.

`task:ready` is not bookkeeping — the pick admits on that label alone, so an item merely
stripped of `task:blocked` wears no state any executor selects on, and the run reports
`nothing ready to pick up`, indistinguishable from a healthy idle run. Waking an item means
stripping `task:blocked` **and** adding `task:ready`.

**`ready-for-agent` and `ready-for-agent-fleet` are triggers**, so they belong on dispatch
issues alone — never on an ordinary issue, from a task or by hand. Applying one starts a
session that will find no valid dispatch and stop. `agent-running` and `needs-human` carry
no trigger and are the right vocabulary for a task marking its own issue as claimed or
handed to a human; a task reusing them owns their whole lifecycle, since the backstop only
converges Claudinite's own items.

## Every exit is terminal

- Success → the item closes with its outcome label and a comment naming what it did.
- Failure → one comment naming what failed, `needs-human`. Nothing keeps updating an issue
  about a failed state — one visible convergence, then it is a human's (or the janitor's).
- **Task gone** (the item names a task the repo no longer carries — file removed, pack
  undeclared) → the executor closes it as not planned. An obsolete item is not an anomaly;
  it gets no `needs-human`.
- Every terminal state is recorded in code as a `claudinite-task-exec` line so the usage
  fold counts task statuses deterministically.

Claiming an item swaps its label, and a label change is itself a triggering event, so the
swap can re-fire the webhook that started you. Judge a duplicate notification by
**ownership**: if the claim comment is yours, this is your own echo — change nothing extra,
don't re-resolve, and keep running the work you already own.

- **Suspend** — set the repo Actions **variable** `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`. Every
  Claudinite workflow checks it as its first act and exits cleanly having fired nothing. It

  where they are, touching no labels. Clearing it is the whole of resuming: the next tick
  reclaims the claims of runs killed during the hold, wakes what came due, and drains. An
  operator who won't wait dispatches the **scheduler** workflow — the tick-plus-drain pair,
  not the bare executor, whose run would drain ready items but skip the reclaim/ready half.
- **Dormancy** — a project nobody is working on declares it in `.claudinite-checks.json`:

  "dormant": true
  ```

  sessions are unaffected. Delete it to wake. Dormancy is a declared standing state in
  tracked config; the suspend variable is the instant, out-of-band operational hold.

## The scheduler workflow

The vendored `claudinite-scheduler.yml` is a thin shim: a `concurrency` group, a
`workflow_dispatch` trigger with the `wake` input, and calls into the vendored engine — no
logic of its own, so schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh rather than
workflow edits.

Its cron is **hourly on a repo-hashed minute in :10–:50**, the one repo-specific value in
the stub (`engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives). Hashing is what staggers the fleet, so an
off-band or duplicated cron breaks staggering and double-run safety. This is the repo's only
cron — the tick is the one thing that needs a clock, and everything a repo does recurringly
reaches Actions through the queue instead of through a workflow of its own.

**Wanting a recurring job to have its own scheduled workflow** — make it a task and delete
the workflow; its steps become the task's prework. Don't keep the workflow as a
dispatch-only shell for the task to fire: that is two files and two edit sites for one job.
The exception is work needing something declared at the *job* level that the scheduler's
jobs don't carry — an `environment:`, an OIDC `id-token` — and even then the task owns the
schedule and the workflow holds only what must be YAML.

  ```

  sessions are unaffected. Delete it to wake. Dormancy is a declared standing state in

The vendored `claudinite-scheduler.yml` is a thin shim: a `concurrency` group, a
`workflow_dispatch` trigger with the `wake` input, and calls into the vendored engine — no
logic of its own, so schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh rather than
workflow edits.

Its cron is **hourly on a repo-hashed minute in :10–:50**, the one repo-specific value in
the stub (`engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives). Hashing is what staggers the fleet, so an

cron — the tick is the one thing that needs a clock, and everything a repo does recurringly

dispatch-only shell for the task to fire: that is two files and two edit sites for one job.

jobs don't carry — an `environment:`, an OIDC `id-token` — and even then the task owns the
schedule and the workflow holds only what must be YAML.

+# Tasks — a repo's unit of Claudinite work

+A **task** is a unit of work a repo does to itself, declared in code and executed in the
+repo's own GitHub Actions run. Most tasks are a deterministic script; some also need an
+agent. Some recur on a clock; others exist only to be created by hand or by another task.
+None of that is in the definition — a task is the declaration plus the work, and everything
+else is how one particular occurrence got started.
+
+An occurrence of a task is a **work item**: a GitHub issue titled `[claudinite-work]
+<pack>/<task>`, whose number is its identity. The queue *is* the repo's issue list — no
+plan file, no watermark, no ledger. The engine is vendored under
+`.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`; the basics pack owns the conformance guards for the
+surfaces a repo authors around it, present wherever basics is declared (everywhere).

+## Four roles, strictly separated
+

+   list: *instantiate* each recurring task's standing item when its anchor comes, *ready*
+   blocked items whose dependencies resolved and whose `Not-before` has passed, and
+   *reclaim* dead executor claims. It evaluates no preconditions, collects no signals, and
+   executes nothing.
+2. **Executors** — pull workers, any number of them. Each iteration picks the next ready
+   item (urgent first), claims it, evaluates the precondition — the only place it is ever
+   evaluated — then runs the work step and either finishes the item or hands it to an
+   agent. A no-go rolls the item to its next anchor. An executor's whole interface is issue
+   read/write plus the repo at HEAD; more capacity is more executors.
+3. **Agents** — one session per handed-off item, invoked by the executor. An agent executes
+   its one item's task file, verifies its outcome ceiling, and converges the item.
+4. **The janitor** — dead executor claims, dead agent claims, stale-item escalation, queue
+   health review.

+tick just created, which is what holds common-case latency at zero without depending on a
+label event being delivered.

+nothing else, which makes it the ordinary way to run a deterministic job in Actions without
+authoring a workflow for it.

+remainder by requesting the agentic phase (`CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`) — for **work prework
+could not do**, never for a re-check of whether the run should have happened.

# core — working with Claudinite itself

Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration, adoption, the
self-refresh, and the contract a scheduled task is written to.

- **Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite** — it is vendored, under
  `.claudinite/shared/`, and the update flows replace that whole tree. Never edit anything there:
  change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.

- **Finding a mounted skill, or following a link from inside one you already loaded** — a canon
  skill lives at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; there is no flat
  `.claudinite/shared/skills/`. When the `Skill` tool announces a per-session flat "base directory"
  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.

- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-checks.json`. Nothing
  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.

- **Adding a pack** — run the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions,
  re-vendors and scaffolds. Never hand-copy a pack's content into the repo.

- **Setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time** — the `adopt-claudinite` skill.

- **Deciding which pack owns a lesson** — read `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of
  *every* canon pack, never the mounted subset: the mount holds only what this repo declares, so the
  pack that owns the territory may be absent and invisible. When the owning pack is merely too
  narrow, widen its `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` rather than opening a local pack beside it.

- **Judging whether Claudinite is current here** — read the stamp's `ref`, `engineVersion` and
  `packVersions`, never `claudinite.updated` on its own: a held stamp pins `updated` behind a
  pending note while the mount keeps converging normally, so it looks stalest when it is fine.

- **Writing or changing a scheduled task** — [tasks.md](tasks.md) is the
  contract, and the precondition is the only place a task may decide not to run.

- **Answering "why did the mount not update"** — read the member's own artifacts (its declaration,
  its stamp, the head sha's runs) before theorizing about a platform setting; propose a settings
  change as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.

---
name: github-actions-scheduling
description: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
---

# GitHub Actions cron is best-effort

GitHub's `schedule:` trigger is a **request to queue**, not a promise to run. A cron'd workflow
routinely fires minutes to tens of minutes late, and under load GitHub **drops** a firing
outright — the run never happens, with no failure, no notification, and nothing in the run
ledger to look at. The effect is worst at `:00` and other round minutes, where everyone's cron
lands at once. GitHub's docs concede only that a schedule "may be delayed during periods of high
loads"; the behaviour is measured across a fleet in
[Upptime's write-up](https://upptime.js.org/blog/2021/01/22/github-actions-schedule-not-working/).
Same family, different mechanism: GitHub **disables** a repo's scheduled workflows entirely
after 60 days without repository activity.

## Building for it

- **Never let correctness depend on a firing happening, or on when it happened.** Derive what is
  due from durable state the run can read — the Actions run ledger, a timestamp in the repo, the
  world the job inspects — never from "this fired, so it must be time". Wall-clock equality with
  the cron minute is not a test any real run passes.
- **Idempotent and self-catching.** A scheduled job does whatever is outstanding *now*, so a
  missed firing costs latency rather than data. Per-tick bookkeeping — counters, "the last hour's
  changes", a queue advanced one step per run — loses information the first time a tick vanishes.
  If a job cannot catch up, say so where it is declared and design the miss as an accepted loss.
- **Catch up the most recent slot only.** A job that backfills every missed slot turns an outage
  into a storm on recovery; one catch-up evaluation per frequency is the shape that survives a
  multi-day gap.
- **Spacing two jobs apart is not an ordering.** "B is an hour after A, so A has finished by
  then" holds only while the fires land on time — and when a poll is dropped, the catch-up run
  finds *both* due and does them together, which is precisely the run where B most needs A to
  have gone first. If the order actually matters, assert it in the run: have the run do A and
  defer B, or have B check for A's result and skip when it is missing. Spacing is a preference;
  a check is a guarantee.
- **Pick a minute off `:00`.** Anywhere in `:10–:50` dodges the stampede and stays clear of the
  hour boundary any slot math anchors on; across a fleet, hash the repo name into that band so
  members spread rather than collide.
- **Deadline-bound work does not belong on a cron.** If something must happen *at* a time, drive
  it from the event, not an hourly poll that may skip.

## Talking about it

- **Say "about hourly, best-effort", never "hourly".** Stating an interval the platform does not
  honour turns ordinary jitter into a bug report.
- **A late or missing run is not a defect until proven one.** First question: did GitHub fire at
  all — check the workflow's run list, not the job's logic. Then: has the repo been quiet for 60
  days? Only after both does the code become a suspect. A single missed slot is expected
  behaviour.

Claudinite's own scheduler is built to this: a repo-hashed `:10–:50` minute, due-slot math
against the Actions run ledger rather than the clock, and most-recent-slot-only catch-up — see
[tasks.md](../../../core/tasks.md) for the task-authoring side.

# core

Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.

**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `core-declared`
reports it.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`core-declared`) |
| Adding a pack | medium | complexity | prose: 27 words |
| Setting a project up on Claudinite | medium | complexity | prose: 15 words |
| Deciding which pack owns a lesson | medium | complexity | prose: 59 words |
| Judging whether Claudinite is current here | medium | correctness | prose: 43 words |
| Writing or changing a scheduled task | high | correctness | prose: 26 words + checks (`task-declaration-shape`, `task-declaration-matches-folder`) |
| Answering "why did the mount not update" | medium | correctness | prose: 39 words |

## Checks

Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `core-declared` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `rules-index-current` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `claudinite-isolation` | high | complexity | check: blocking |
| `conformance-workflow` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-declaration-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-declaration-matches-folder` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-phase-discipline` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |

What goes wrong when one fires:

- `core-declared` — this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-checks.json`, so none of the rules above run and the session cannot tell.
- `rules-index-current` — the generated index is missing, stale or unimported: the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session.
- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` [barrier](../barriers/README.md) edge).
- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.
- `scheduler-workflow-shape` — the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted: staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break.
- `task-declaration-shape` — a task declaration the scheduler reads is incomplete or illegal, so the task never fires or fires wrong.
- `task-declaration-matches-folder` — a declaration disagrees with its folder: discovery drops it into `errors` and every run keeps reporting healthy without it.
- `task-phase-discipline` — a task decides not to run after its precondition already said run, hiding the decision from the run records.

The scope cuts the other way too: a rule about how the **canon's own** content is maintained is not
this pack's, however much it looks like one. `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` lists every
`packs/<name>/` — reads as Claudinite machinery and is not: it can only fire in the corpus repo, and
what it guards is a hand-maintained index, not a member's status. It stays in
[basics](../basics/README.md) with the other doc-integrity rules.

## Skills

| Skill | For |
|---|---|
| [`adopt-claudinite`](skills/adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md) | setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time — mount, hooks, checks, skills — and re-baselining one to pick up updates |
| [`adopt-pack`](skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) | adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land |

The adoption skills bundle two more checks of the same kind, over the answers a member stores
against each declared pack's questions:

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `adoption-answers-pending` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
| `interview-answer-stale` | low | complexity | check: advisory |

## Tasks

| Task | frequency | Runs when |
|---|---|---|
| `update` | daily (02:00 anchor) | the mount is behind the canon, or a declared pack moved |
| `adopt-requested-packs` | daily | the repo carries an open pack-adoption request |

`update` is the per-repo self-refresh — the task that converges a member's mount and stamps it. It
is why `core-declared` is blocking: a member runs `update` from its **vendored** copy, and
`discoverTasks` finds only a literally-declared pack's tasks, so a repo that loses this pack's entry
loses its self-refresh, and nothing is left that could deliver it one. That is also why the task
arrived here a change later than the rest of the pack — it moved only once every non-dormant member's
declaration had been read back and confirmed to carry `core`.

4	pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.

7	declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it

9	reports it.
10	
11	## Rules (`RULES.md`)

14	|---|---|---|---|
15	| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
16	| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |

27	
28	Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
29	converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
30	not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.
31	
32	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
33	|---|---|---|---|
34	| `core-declared` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
35	| `rules-index-current` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |

37	| `conformance-workflow` | high | correctness | check: advisory |

44	
45	- `core-declared` — this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-checks.json`, so none of the rules above run and the session cannot tell.
46	- `rules-index-current` — the generated index is missing, stale or unimported: the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session.
47	- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` [barrier](../barriers/README.md) edge).
48	- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.
49	- `scheduler-workflow-shape` — the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted: staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break.
50	- `task-declaration-shape` — a task declaration the scheduler reads is incomplete or illegal, so the task never fires or fires wrong.
51	- `task-declaration-matches-folder` — a declaration disagrees with its folder: discovery drops it into `errors` and every run keeps reporting healthy without it.

input.body:
Fixes #972.

`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md` is what a session reads before writing or changing a task. It described the **slot** mechanism — now the legacy opt-out, since `dispatchMode` defaults to `queue` — and taught two wrong models along the way.

## What was wrong

**"A task is agentic work."** The doc led with a scheduler that "creates dispatch issues (`ready-for-agent`) for agentic work" and filed `agent_model: none` as a footnote. `engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs` runs prework in the drain job and, absent an agent request, closes the item right there: *"Prework did this run's work; no agent was needed."* A deterministic script running in Actions with no workflow file of its own is the ordinary shape of a task.

**"A task is a scheduled run."** The title said so, and the framing hung every task off the hourly cron. The tick only instantiates *recurring* items; items come equally from `create-work-item`, a `wake` dispatch, and another task's fan-out, and `manual` tasks are never instantiated by the tick at all.

The "the repo's **only** cron" sentence sat in the middle of that and read as the definition of a task.

## What changed

`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md` → [`packs/core/tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/github-pages-deploy-action-8l1dtr/packs/core/tasks.md), rewritten in the present tense:

- Opens on what a task is — a unit of the repo's own work, executed in the repo's Actions run — with the agentic phase and the recurring anchor each named as optional.
- Four roles (generator / executors / agents / janitor), and the tick-then-drain pair that holds latency at zero without depending on a label event.
- **The work step is code; the agent is the escalation** — including the prework-then-`CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT` shape and why the secrets story means a workflow that exists only to hold a secret is redundant.
- **Where an item comes from** — four origins, equal in standing, with `manual` explained rather than mentioned.
- The declaration contract, the precondition-is-the-only-decision-point rule with `exclusive`, the label vocabulary (including why `task:ready` is not bookkeeping), terminal exits, and suspend vs. dormancy.
- **The scheduler workflow** section keeps the one-cron invariant — still enforced by `engine/selftest.mjs`, unchanged — as what it is: a property of that workflow. The "make it a task, delete the workflow" rule lives there too, with the exception stated precisely as *what must be declared at the job level and the scheduler's jobs don't carry* (an `environment:`, an OIDC `id-token`).

Retired along the way, per the authoring rule against narrating a superseded practice: the slot vocabulary, "re-arming lost trigger events" as a janitor job, and the executor-as-label-fired-routine description.

`core/RULES.md` splits its one task rule in two, so the reader who wants a job to run in Actions — and would otherwise author a workflow — is caught by a rule keyed to what they are doing.

## Sweep

`scheduled-tasks.md` → `tasks.md` across 17 files, including the `doc:` field of four checks. `docs/per-project-scheduling/` is a historical record — link targets updated, content untouched. Also corrected: the `github-actions-scheduling` skill's closing paragraph, which described the retired due-slot-against-the-run-ledger math; `packs/core/README.md`'s rule index and its `02:00 slot` → `02:00 anchor`; the concept name at four other reference sites.

Version bumped on `core`, `github-actions`, `product-wiki`, `sheepdog`.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2099 pass, 0 fail.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs --changed --base origin/main` — exit 0.

Both failed first (`rule-index` on the added rule, `pack-version-bumped` on four packs) and were fixed rather than worked around.

## One thing I assumed

You called the "only cron" line annoying. I read that as the *framing* — it was being used to define a task — not as a request to allow a second cron, so the invariant and its selftest are untouched and the sentence now appears once, in the scheduler-workflow section. Say the word if you meant the invariant itself.

---

You were right on both counts, and the doc was the reason I was wrong. [`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`](packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) still described the **slot** mechanism — `dispatchMode` in `engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs` has defaulted to `queue` for a while — so it taught a scheduler that "creates dispatch issues for agentic work" with `agent_model: none` as a footnote, and hung every task off the cron. The engine says the opposite: `queue/executor.mjs` runs prework in the drain job and closes the item there with *"Prework did this run's work; no agent was needed."*

[`core/RULES.md`](packs/core/RULES.md) now also carries a rule keyed to *wanting a job to run in Actions*, so the next session reaches for a task instead of a workflow.

On the "only cron" line — I kept the invariant (it's enforced by `engine/selftest.mjs`) but demoted it to the scheduler-workflow section where it's a fact about that file, not the definition of a task. If you meant the invariant itself should go, that's a different change and I haven't made it.

Back to your original question with the corrected model: the privacy Pages deploy **could** be a task's `prework`, and my earlier "tasks are agentic" reasoning was wrong. What actually stops it is narrower — `environment: github-pages` and `id-token: write` are job-level declarations the drain job doesn't carry. That's the exception the new doc states, not the sweeping one I gave you. Whether to widen the drain job or leave the deploy as YAML is a real open question I haven't filed.

> ⚠️ Still open: [PR #975](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/975) needs review. Two things I did not decide for you — whether the one-cron invariant itself should go, and whether the Pages deploy is worth converting now that the only blocker is two job-level declarations.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.

# Scheduled tasks — the per-project scheduling mechanism

How a repo's recurring Claudinite work runs. A repo schedules **itself**, and
every occurrence of every task is an **issue in that repo** — a `[claudinite-work]`
work item whose labels are its state. That is the work-item queue; what follows is
the contract a task is written to, not how the queue works internally.

Three responsibilities, strictly separated (owner, 2026-08-06):

1. **The tick** — a vendored hourly Action
   (`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) that is pure label mechanics
   over the issue list: **instantiate** each recurring task's standing item when
   its anchor comes, **ready** blocked items whose wait has passed, **reclaim**
   dead executor claims. It evaluates no precondition and collects no signal.
2. **The executor** — a pull worker over the queue (the tick's post-tick drain,
   and a `labeled`-event run for latency) that picks the next ready item, claims
   it, evaluates **that one task's** precondition, runs its prework, and either
   converges the item or hands off to an agent session.
3. **The task-janitor** — an ordinary daily task (`basics/task-janitor`,
   `agent_model: none`) that owns everything about the queue that is *nobody's

  minute constrained to **:10–:50** (the one repo-specific value in the stub —

Both guards are **relevance-first**: inert until their artifact exists, so
on a repo with neither artifact they are a no-op.

## The task folder

One directory per task — `<pack>/tasks/<name>/` — holding **`task.mjs`** (the
self-contained declaration + `precondition(signals, config)`, the eligibility
gate as pure code) beside **`task.md`** (the worker spec the executing agent
follows), plus any deterministic helpers. The precondition both asserts
need-to-run and pre-decides scope: its `context` lines join the item's own
Context as binding constraints the agent may not re-litigate. `agent_model:
none` replaces the worker doc with an inline `.mjs` the executor runs as prework
— no agent phase, and the item closes on that subprocess's outcome. This is the
scheduled-task shape of the unattended-agents routine-folder convention; the
issue-driven-dispatch security rule (the issue is data, the task path is
code-validated, agent_model/expected_outcome come from the repo) lives with that
skill's agent practices.

### Three optional declarations

Declare one only when its rule applies.

python3 - <<'PY'
p='packs/core/tasks.md'
s=open(p).read()
anchor = "## The precondition is the ONLY decision point"
section = """## Where an item comes from

Creating an item, or waking one that already exists, is the whole of urgency,
forcing, fan-out and retry. Four origins, equal in standing — a recurring anchor is
one of them, not the definition of a task:

- **A recurring task's anchor** — the tick instantiates the standing item. The
  item carries `origin:schedule`, which is what makes it count as that occurrence.
- **By hand** — the operator lever, run from the repo:

  ```
  node engine/scheduler/queue/create-work-item.mjs <pack>/<task> [--urgent] [--context …] [--qualifier text] [--supersedes #N]
  node engine/scheduler/queue/create-work-item.mjs --wake <#N> [--urgent]
  ```

  Creating names ad-hoc work — a parameterized run, a `manual` task, a fan-out
  target — and carries no `origin:schedule`, so it neither suppresses tomorrow's
  occurrence nor consumes it. Waking forces a standing item that already exists,
  and is the same operation as re-queueing one out of `needs-human`.
- **A `wake` dispatch of the scheduler workflow** — the same wake, reachable from
  outside the repo. The fleet enforcer dispatches a member's own scheduler naming
  the tasks, and the member applies it with its own token, rather than the
  enforcer holding issue writes on every repository.
- **Another task** — a fan-out creates one item per target, told apart by
  `--qualifier`.

**`frequency: 'manual'` is a task the tick never instantiates**: its items come
only from the other three. Declare it for work that has no anchor — something an
operator or an upstream task asks for — and it costs nothing on the cycles nobody
asks.

Whatever the origin, the executor evaluates the precondition at pick. A force that
finds no work says so where the operator reads it, rather than running anyway.

"""
assert anchor in s
s = s.replace(anchor, section + anchor, 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")
PY

content.content:
Claudinite's own scheduler is built to this: a repo-hashed `:10–:50` minute, and an hourly tick
that reconciles a queue of issues rather than replaying a ledger — a missed fire leaves the queue
exactly as it was, so the next one catches up by looking at it. See
[tasks.md](../../../core/tasks.md) for the task-authoring side.
=== core RULES ===
- **Writing or changing a task** — [tasks.md](tasks.md) is the contract, and the precondition
  is the only place a task may decide not to run. A task is a unit of the repo's own work, not
  a synonym for agentic work or for a cron: most are a deterministic script the executor runs
  in Actions, and an agentic phase and a recurring anchor are each optional.

- **Wanting a job to run in Actions** — make it a task and give it a `prework`
  command; the vendored scheduler already owns the trigger, the concurrency and the failure
  reporting. Author a workflow only for what must be declared at the *job* level and the
  scheduler's jobs don't carry — an `environment:`, an OIDC `id-token` — and keep the schedule
  with the task even then.

input.body:
Fixes #972. Rebased onto `main` after #993 (slot retirement) and #941 — which rewrote most of this doc. Re-verified against the new base, and **the change is much smaller than the one I first pushed.**

## What the rebase changed about this PR

`main` already fixed the *mechanism* half: tick/executor/janitor, the queue labels, granular label writes, the nonce hand-off, `after` replacing the exclusive-run claim, the item lifecycle with roll. That is better than what I had written, and it carries facts I didn't have. My original rewrite is discarded in favour of it — including two things I had documented that **do not exist**: `exclusive` (retired with the slot scheduler) and `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL` (designed, never implemented). The diff is now a 77%-similarity rename rather than a rewrite.

What survived is the half `main` did not do — the two assumptions in the framing.

## Still needed, and now the whole change

"A task is a scheduled run."** The title said so; the doc opened "How a repo's recurring Claudinite work runs." `frequency: 'manual'` appeared only inside the frequency enum, and `create-work-item` only as a retry path — so the origins that aren't the clock were invisible. # Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

1	# Tasks — a repo's unit of Claudinite work
2	
3	A **task** is a unit of work a repo does to itself, declared in code and executed in
4	that repo's own GitHub Actions run. Most tasks are a deterministic script; some also
5	need an agent. Some recur on a clock; others exist only to be created by hand or by
6	another task. None of that is in the definition — a task is the declaration plus the
7	work, and everything else is how one occurrence of it got started.
8	
9	Every occurrence is an **issue in that repo** — a `[claudinite-work]` work item whose
10	labels are its state. That is the work-item queue; what follows is the contract a task
11	is written to, not how the queue works internally.
12	
13	Three responsibilities, strictly separated (owner, 2026-08-06):
14	
15	1. **The tick** — a vendored hourly Action
16	   (`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) that is pure label mechanics
17	   over the issue list: **instantiate** each recurring task's standing item when
18	   its anchor comes, **ready** blocked items whose wait has passed, **reclaim**
19	   dead executor claims. It evaluates no precondition and collects no signal.
20	2. **The executor** — a pull worker over the queue (the tick's post-tick drain,
21	   and a `labeled`-event run for latency) that picks the next ready item, claims
22	   it, evaluates **that one task's** precondition, runs its prework, and either
23	   converges the item or hands off to an agent session.
24	3. **The task-janitor** — an ordinary daily task (`basics/task-janitor`,
25	   `agent_model: none`) that owns everything about the queue that is *nobody's
26	   task*: items stuck ready past their period, items wearing no state label after
27	   a torn transition, and a health review of the open set.
28	
29	The engine is vendored under `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`; the basics
30	pack owns the conformance guards for the surfaces a repo authors around it —
31	scheduling is baseline Claudinite discipline, present wherever basics is
32	declared (everywhere), not an opt-in feature.
33	
34	There is no watermark and no per-run state: an occurrence exists because its
35	issue exists, which is why an outage self-heals by looking at the queue rather
36	than by replaying a ledger.
37	
38	## What the checks guard
39	
40	- **The scheduler workflow is a thin shim.** The vendored
41	  `claudinite-scheduler.yml` carries a single **hourly** cron on a repo-hashed
42	  minute constrained to **:10–:50** (the one repo-specific value in the stub —
43	  `engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
44	  bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives), a `concurrency` group, a
45	  `workflow_dispatch` trigger (whose one `wake` input is how a task is forced,
46	  here or from another repo), and a call into the vendored tick — no logic of its own
47	  (schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh, not workflow edits). It
48	  is the repo's **only** cron; the executor's workflow beside it carries none. That is
49	  a property of this workflow, not a definition of a task — the tick is the one thing
50	  needing a clock, and everything else reaches Actions through the queue. Off-band or
51	  multiple crons, or a missing concurrency/dispatch guard, break staggering, double-run
52	  safety, or manual runs.
53	
54	- **Work a repo does to itself needs no workflow of its own.** Make it a task with a
55	  `prework` command: the vendored workflows already own the trigger, the concurrency,
56	  the secrets and the failure reporting, and prework is an ordinary subprocess in their
57	  Actions run. Don't keep a workflow as a dispatch-only shell for the task to fire —
58	  that is two files and two edit sites for one job. The exception is what must be
59	  declared at the **job** level and these jobs don't carry: an `environment:`, an OIDC
60	  `id-token`. Then the workflow holds only that, and the task still owns the schedule.
61	
62	- **Every task declaration carries the full contract.** A `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`
63	  default-exports `id` (matching its directory), `frequency` (`hourly | daily-2h
64	  | daily-1h | daily | daily+1h | weekly | monthly | manual`), `precondition_signals` (the collector
65	  vocabulary), `agent_model` (`opus | sonnet | haiku | none`), `expected_outcome` (`none |
66	  open-pr | merged-pr`), and a `precondition`. An agentic task (`agent_model !==
67	  none`) also carries `agent_instructions`, the worker file the agent reads; a
68	  `none` task runs no agent, so the field is not applicable and is omitted. The
69	  tick and executor read agent_model/expected_outcome/frequency from this file — never from the work
70	  item — so an illegal or missing value means a task never fires, fires wrong,
71	  or writes past its declared ceiling. The same contract
72	  (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs`) is re-validated at run time, so the
73	  static and runtime views can't drift. A task declares **no session scope** — see
74	  the next entry.
75	
76	- **A task's code reads only the environment prework is handed.** Prework runs as
77	  a subprocess with a fixed set of `CLAUDINITE_*` variables — `REPO_ROOT`, `REPO`,
78	  `DEFAULT_BRANCH`, `ITEM`, `PACK`, `TASK`, `CONTEXT`, `REQUEST_AGENT` — and
79	  `task-prework-env` (blocking) rejects a read of anything else. A variable nobody
80	  sets is `undefined`, the parse of it yields empty, and the run goes green having
81	  quietly done something other than what it was asked: that is how three fleet
82	  tasks kept taking their parameters through a channel the queue had stopped
83	  setting, leaving a fleet-wide sweep unable to be scoped or dry-run. **Operator
84	  parameters ride the item's Context** (`CLAUDINITE_CONTEXT`, one line per bullet),
85	  which is the only channel a task may take them from.
86	
87	- **Session scope is retired, and `session_scope` is now inert** (owner ruling,
88	  2026-08-09; the field's last reader went with the slot scheduler). Reach is a
89	  property of **which endpoint the hand-off calls** — `invocation_endpoint`, below
90	  — so a task needing wider access names a different endpoint and nothing else in
91	  the system has a concept of scope. A declaration still carrying `session_scope`
92	  validates and does nothing at all; `task-declaration-shape` raises it as an
93	  advisory rename (advisory on purpose: a member's vendor refresh must not turn its
94	  CI red over a file nothing has edited yet). Drop it, and name an endpoint if the
95	  task actually needed the reach.
96	
97	- **Every run is bounded.** An agentic task (`agent_model !== none`) declares
98	  `agent_execution_timeout` — seconds bounding the agentic run
99	  (task-prework design §2, §6 — see issue #394).
100	  There is no platform wall-clock kill for a launched agent session, so the
101	  bound is best-effort: the hand-off surfaces it into the session's brief ("fail
102	  after N minutes") and the agent leash catches a session that never converges its
103	  item. Set it generously — extreme protection against a runaway, not a scheduling
104	  knob.
105	
106	- **A task says which repo secrets it needs.** Prework runs Action-side, so repo
107	  Actions secrets are reachable there and nowhere else in a task's life (an agent
108	  session carries none). A task lists what it needs in `required_secrets`; the
109	  wiring converge stamps each name into the workflows that run prework — the tick's
110	  drain and the executor — so a worker reads it as ordinary environment. A declared
111	  secret the repo has not configured is **named, not guessed at**: prework is the
112	  only code that sees a secret's value, so the executor converges the item to
113	  `needs-human` saying exactly which one is missing. Nothing else fails; the task
114	  that needs the secret just doesn't work yet. The consequence worth designing
115	  around: **a workflow that exists only to hold a secret is redundant** — fold its
116	  work into the task's prework rather than dispatching and polling a second
117	  workflow from an agent.
118	
119	- **A standing tracker belongs to the task that keeps one, not to the machinery.**

- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.

Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.

- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. - repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. # Tasks — the per-project work mechanism

How a repo's own Claudinite work runs. A repo schedules **itself**, and
every occurrence of every task is an **issue in that repo** — a `[claudinite-work]`
work item whose labels are its state. That is the work-item queue; what follows is
the contract a task is written to, not how the queue works internally.

**A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is.** A task is a
unit of the repo's own work with a precondition, a code-work phase and optionally an
agentic-work phase; `frequency` says only how often the queue offers to run it, and
`manual` — no cadence at all — is a first-class value. Work that fires on an event,
on a condition, or on a force is a task in exactly the same sense as work that fires
nightly, and reads the same contract. Anything reachable from the executor belongs
here rather than in a workflow of its own; see the cron rule below for the narrow
case that genuinely cannot be.

Three responsibilities, strictly separated (owner, 2026-08-06):

1. **The tick** — a vendored hourly Action
   (`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) that is pure label mechanics
   over the issue list: **instantiate** each recurring task's standing item when
   its anchor comes, **ready** blocked items whose wait has passed, **reclaim**
   dead executor claims. It evaluates no precondition and collects no signal.
2. **The executor** — a pull worker over the queue (the tick's post-tick drain,
   and a `labeled`-event run for latency) that picks the next ready item, claims
   it, evaluates **that one task's** precondition, runs its code-work, and either
   converges the item or hands off to an agent session.
3. **The task-janitor** — an ordinary daily task (`basics/task-janitor`,
   `agent_model: none`) that owns everything about the queue that is *nobody's
   task*: items stuck ready past their period, items wearing no state label after
   a torn transition, and a health review of the open set.

The engine is vendored under `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`; the basics
pack owns the conformance guards for the surfaces a repo authors around it —
scheduling is baseline Claudinite discipline, present wherever basics is
declared (everywhere), not an opt-in feature.

There is no watermark and no per-run state: an occurrence exists because its
issue exists, which is why an outage self-heals by looking at the queue rather
than by replaying a ledger.

content.content:
## What the checks guard

- **The scheduler workflow is a thin shim.** The vendored
  `claudinite-scheduler.yml` carries a single **hourly** cron on a repo-hashed
  minute constrained to **:10–:50** (the one repo-specific value in the stub —
  `engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
  bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives), a `concurrency` group, a
  `workflow_dispatch` trigger (whose one `wake` input is how a task is forced,
  here or from another repo), and a call into the vendored tick — no logic of its own
  (schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh, not workflow edits). It
  is the repo's **only** cron; the executor's workflow beside it carries none. Work
  that had its own cron'd workflow becomes a **task**, and that workflow is deleted
  — its steps move into the task's worker. So does work with no cron at all: an
  event-driven or condition-gated job becomes a task on `frequency: 'manual'`, woken
  by whatever knows the event happened. Don't keep either as a dispatch-only workflow
  for the task to fire: that is two files and two edit sites for one job, and a
  workflow whose only caller is the thing that replaced it. (A workflow that must run
  *as an Action* for something a task cannot reach — an Actions-only secret, an OIDC
  identity a deploy target demands — is the exception. Even then the task owns the
  trigger and the decision to run; the workflow carries only the step that needs the
  Action's own privileges.) Off-band or multiple
  crons, or a missing concurrency/dispatch guard, break staggering, double-run
  safety, or manual runs.

- **Every task declaration carries the full contract.** A `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`
## The task folder

One directory per task — `<pack>/tasks/<name>/` — holding **`task.mjs`** (the
self-contained declaration + `precondition(signals, config)`, the eligibility
gate as pure code) beside **`task.md`** (the worker spec the executing agent
follows), plus any deterministic helpers. The precondition both asserts
need-to-run and pre-decides scope: its `context` lines join the item's own
Context as binding constraints the agent may not re-litigate. `agent_model:
none` replaces the worker doc with an inline `.mjs` the executor runs as code-work
— no agent phase, and the item closes on that subprocess's outcome. This is the
scheduled-task shape of the unattended-agents routine-folder convention; the
issue-driven-dispatch security rule (the issue is data, the task path is
code-validated, agent_model/expected_outcome come from the repo) lives with that
skill's agent practices.

### Three optional declarations

1	# core
2	
3	Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
4	pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every task is written to.
5	
6	**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
7	declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
8	into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `core-declared`
9	reports it.
10	
11	## Rules (`RULES.md`)
12	
13	| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
14	|---|---|---|---|
15	| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
16	| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
17	| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`core-declared`) |
